1:1.t: We wish to interpret Malachi, the last of the twelve prophets, whose name the LXX translated "his angel", saying: The taking up of the word of the Lord upon Israel in the hand of his angel, in place of which we read in the Hebrew Malachi, which is more correctly and expressly rendered "angel", that is, "my messenger". Nor is it to be thought, according to the opinion of some, that an angel came from heaven and took up a human body, in order to speak to Israel the things that had been commanded by the Lord. […]

The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel, in the hand of Malachi. LXX: The taking up of the word of the Lord upon Israel, in the hand of his angel. What burden signifies, that is, weight, which in Hebrew is called massa and by Aquila ἄρμα, or what λῆμμα signifies, that is, taking up, which both the Seventy and the other translators rendered, we have said in other prophets. For Nahum too writes: The burden of Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite, and Habakkuk: The burden which Habakkuk the prophet saw, and Zechariah: The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and of Damascus his rest. And again in what follows: The burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel. […]

LXX: Set it upon your hearts. This is not found in the Hebrew, but I think it was added from Haggai, in whom we read: And now set it upon your hearts from this day and upward. After the title of the prophet, then, or the preface, this is to be taken in two ways: Set it upon your hearts, that is, take note of and consider that which was said above: The taking up of the word of the Lord upon Israel in the hand of his angel. Or else: take careful note of the things that are to be said afterward, so that you may know them not with the ears of the body but with the understanding of the mind and heart, and may make for yourselves treasuries in which to receive the riches of the words of God, and wisdom may act with confidence when you have been enlarged, and, your heart filled with the […]

1:2.t: And in both directions, before the little ones were born: "God loved Jacob, but Esau he held in hatred" (Mal. 1:1, 2). Here the heretics find an opening, who claim that there are diverse natures, namely the spiritual and the animal and the χοϊκὴν (earthy), and that one is saved, another perishes, and another stands between the two; for, they say, neither would the righteous man ever be chosen before he had done anything good, nor the sinner be hated before his sin, unless the nature of those who perish and of those who are to be saved were different. […]

I have loved you, says the Lord. And you have said: In what have you loved us? Was not Esau the brother of Jacob, says the Lord, and I have loved Jacob, but Esau I have hated? And I have made his mountains a wilderness, and his inheritance a place for the dragons of the desert. But if Idumea should say: We are destroyed, but returning we will build the things that are destroyed; thus says the Lord of hosts: They will build, and I will destroy; and they shall be called the borders of impiety, and the people with whom the Lord is angry for ever. And your eyes shall see, and you shall say: May the Lord be magnified upon the border of Israel. LXX: I have loved you, says the Lord, and you have said: In what have you loved us? Was not Esau the brother of Jacob, says the Lord; […]

Now let us come to the spiritual understanding. Israel, a man or a mind seeing God, or, as I think better, εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ, that is, most upright of God, is loved by the Lord, and wishes to know the reason for his love toward him. And the Lord answered that Esau and Jacob were begotten of one stock, that is, that vices and virtues proceed from the one fountain of the heart, since by the freedom of choice we incline to either side as we will; but the vices are born first, through infancy, childhood and youth, and afterward a firmer age reproves and supplants them. The elder brother is hairy and bloody with his hunting, and delights in woods and beasts. The younger is smooth and simple, and dwells innocently at home. […]

Furthermore, who would be so impiously foolish as to say that God cannot turn the evil wills of people—as he wills, when he wills and where he wills—toward the good? But when he acts, he acts through mercy; when he does not act, it is through justice. For "he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills, he hardens." Now when the apostle said this, he was commending grace, of which he had just spoken in connection with the twin children in Rebecca's womb: "Before they had yet been born or had done anything good or bad, in order that the electing purpose of God might continue, it was said of them, 'The elder shall serve the younger.' " Accordingly he refers to another prophetic witness, where it is written, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I have hated." […]

Who are these that reply to God, who speaks to Rebecca? She had twin sons of one conception of Isaac our father. "The children were not yet born nor had done any good or evil (that the purpose of God according to election might stand)." The election was of grace, not of merit. It is the election by which he does not find but makes elect—"that it was not of works but of him that calls, that the elder should serve the younger." To this sentence the blessed apostle adds the testimony of a prophet who came along afterward: "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated" to give us to understand plainly by the later utterance what was hidden in the predestination of God by grace before they were born. […]

1:4.t: But if Edom, that is, Esau, should say: we have indeed been destroyed, unto the wrath of God, but we will build the cities again, know this from the Lord's foretelling, that as they build, I will destroy, and their everlasting desolation will prove my wrath.

The Jews falsely flatter themselves that the Romans are prophesied as Edom, and they themselves as Israel, at the consummation of the world, on the ground that once the Roman empire, that is, the Idumean, has been destroyed, the kingdom of the world will come to the Jews. These things we have said as well as we could, laying the foundations of the history.

1:5.t: So I have shown my hatred toward Esau in deeds, but my love toward you, that is, toward Jacob, I will prove by what follows. When they have been destroyed and reduced to a wilderness, your eyes will see, and you will say: May the Lord be magnified upon the border of Israel; and from the comparison with the evils your brother suffers, you will feel the benefits of God toward you.

1:6.t: And, in short, I perceive three different dispositions which by inevitable necessity lead us to obey. Either through fear of punishment we turn away from that which is evil, and so are of a slavish disposition; or, seeking to profit by the reward, we fulfil the commandments for the sake of our own benefit, and are accordingly like hirelings; or else we do good for the sake of the good itself and from love of Him Who gave us the law, rejoicing that we are thus thought worthy to serve the glorious and great God, and so we have the disposition of sons. Nor will he who keeps the commandments from fear, and is always expecting the penalty of sloth, obey some orders and neglect others, but he will dread as equally terrible the judgment which comes upon every disobedience. […]

There is then on the one hand a natural glory, as light is the glory of the sun; and on the other a glory bestowed judicially and of free will 'ab extra' on them that are worthy. The latter is twofold. "A son," it is said, "honoureth his father, and a servant his master." Of these two the one, the servile, is given by the creature; the other, which may be called the intimate, is fulfilled by the Spirit. For, as our Lord said of Himself, "I have glorified Thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do;" so of the Paraclete He says "He shall glorify me: for He shall receive of mine, and shall show it unto you."

In this world, then, it is thus that men are made slaves, but they who have escaped poverty or war, or do not require the tutelage of others, are free. It follows that even though one man be called master and another servant, nevertheless, both in view of our mutual equality of rank and as chattels of our Creator, we are all fellow slaves. But in that other world what can you bring out of bondage? For no sooner were they created than bondage was commenced. The heavenly bodies exercise no rule over one another, for they are unmoved by ambition, but all bow down to God, and render to Him alike the awe which is due to Him as Master and the glory which falls to Him as Creator. For "a son honoureth his father and a servant his master," and from all God asks one of these two things; […]

And indeed Balaam the prophet, when he had corrupted Israel by Baal-peor, suffered punishment; and Caiaphas at last was his own murderer; and the sons of Sceva, endeavoring to cast out demons, were wounded by them and fled away in an unseemly manner; and the kings of Israel and of Judah, when they became impious, suffered all sorts of punishments. It is therefore evident how bishops and presbyters, also falsely so called, will not escape the judgment of God. For it will be said to them even now: "O you priests that despise my name, I will deliver you up to the slaughter, as I did Zedekiah and Ahab, whom the king of Babylon fried in a frying pan," as says Jeremiah the prophet.

He is God because of fear, but Father for the sake of honor, and because from him is every origin; for he himself said in Malachi the prophet: If I am God, where is my fear? and if I am Father, where is my honor (Mal. 1:6)?

Be obedient to your bishop and obey him as your spiritual father. Sons love and slaves fear. "If I am a father," he says, "where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is my fear?" In your case one man combines in himself many titles to your respect. He is at once monk, bishop and uncle. But the bishops also should know themselves to be priests, not lords. Let them render to the clergy the honor that is their due that the clergy may offer to them the respect which belongs to bishops.

A son honors his father, and a servant his lord; if then I am a father, where is my honor? And if I am a lord, where is my fear? says the Lord of hosts. LXX: A son glorifies his father, and a servant will fear his lord. And if I am a father, where is my glory? And if I am a lord, where is my fear? says the Lord Almighty. Although before you were born I began to love you as sons in Jacob, still, choose by which name you will call me: either I am your father, or your lord. If a father, render the honor due to a father, and offer a devotion worthy of a parent. If a lord, why do you despise me? Why do you not fear your lord? […]

To you, O priests, who despise my name, and you have said: In what have we despised your name?

You offer polluted bread upon my altar, and you say: In what have we polluted you? In that you say: The table of the Lord is despised. LXX: You, O priests, who despise my name, and have said: In what have we despised your name? Offering polluted loaves at my altar; and you have said: In what have we polluted them? In that you say: The table of the Lord is despised. But what follows: And the things set upon it you have despised, we have marked with an obelus, because it is not found in the Hebrew, and was added from what follows. […]

We have drawn faint lines, on which the spiritual explanation is to be impressed. The divine word rebukes negligent bishops, and presbyters and deacons, or else, since we are a priestly and royal race, all who, baptized in Christ, are reckoned by the name of Christ, as to why they despise the name of God; and when they ask in what they have despised his name, it shows them the causes of the offence. You offer, he says, polluted bread upon my altar. We pollute the bread, that is, the body of Christ, when we approach the altar unworthy and, filthy as we are, drink the clean blood, and we say: The table of the Lord is despised; not that anyone would dare to say this, and to utter with criminal voice what he impiously thinks, but the works of sinners despise the table of God. […]

We must consider what it is that we have been commanded to pray for—commanded by him from whom we learn to pray for and through whom we obtain what we pray for. He says, "In this manner shall you pray: 'Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.'?" In every kind of petition we ought first to try to gain the good will of the one we are petitioning. And the praise is usually placed at the beginning of the prayer, where in this instance our Lord has bidden us to say nothing else than "our Father who art in heaven." […]

And if to anyone relying on the help of God and not on his own efforts, it has been vouch-safed to acquire this state, from the condition of a Servant, wherein is fear, and from a mercenary greed of hope, whereby there is sought not so much the good of the donor as the recompense of reward, he will begin to pass on to the adoption of sons, where there is no longer fear, nor greed, but that love which never faileth continually endures. Of which fear and love the Lord in chiding some shows what is befitting for each one: "A son knoweth his own father, and a servant feareth his lord: And if I be a Father, where is My honour: and if I be a Lord, where is my fear?" […]

1:6.t: And therefore there is a twofold stage of fear. The one for beginners, i.e., for those who are still subject to the yoke and to servile terror; of which we read: "And the servant shall fear his Lord;" and in the gospel: "I no longer call you servants, for the servant knoweth not what his Lord doeth;" and therefore "the servant," He tells us, "abideth not in the house for ever, but the Son abideth for ever." For He is instructing us to pass on from that penal fear to the fullest freedom of love, and the confidence of the friends and sons of God. […]

"If I be Lord, where are those who fear Me? And if I be Father, why do ye not honour Me?" Therefore they should either have feared [Him] as Lord, or have honoured [Him] as Father.

1:8.t: WHY WAS ABEL’S SACRIFICE ACCEPTED, AND CAIN’S REJECTED? — This can be gathered from the words of the very passage itself, since the story is not wrapped in literary pretense. For Scripture’s own language shows Abel to be wise and devout in what he did, but Cain careless and thoughtless, and therefore less devout. Abel, then, chose the better parts from the peaceful flock to offer to the Lord his creator, so that from the things God had created he might offer Him the worthiest, thereby proving both his own submission and God’s merit, and showing his personal reverence and God as author of all. Cain, crudely, was unable to present this. Fixing his whole mind in the soil, he could not lift the eyes of his heart to heaven to see what would be worthy of the Creator; […]

1:8.t: If you offer the blind for immolation, is it not evil? And if you offer the lame and the sick, is it not evil? Offer it to your governor, whether it will please him, or whether he will accept your face, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: For if you offer the blind for a sacrifice, is it not evil? And if you offer the lame and the sick, is it not evil? Offer it to your governor, whether he will receive you, whether he will accept your face, says the Lord Almighty. About the diversity of victims, and which ought to be offered and which not, we learn more fully in Leviticus. […]

1:9.t: Moreover, the LXX suggest a far different sense: O priests, who sacrifice feeble sacrificial victims, turn to repentance, and entreat the face of the Lord, and pray for the works of your hands. But as for what he adds: If I shall accept your faces from you, I do not know whether it fits an exhortation to repentance. For no one says: Pray to me, and I will not spare you.

And now entreat the face of God that he may have mercy on you, for by your hand this has been done, if in any way he may accept your faces, says the Lord of hosts. Who is there among you that will shut the doors and kindle my altar gratuitously? LXX: And now entreat the face of your God, and ask him; by your hands these things have been done, if I shall accept your faces from you, says the Lord Almighty, because among you too the doors shall be shut, and my altar shall not be kindled for nothing. In this place the Seventy translators differ widely from the Hebrew truth; and it must be that, where the translation is different, the sense too is different. […]

1:10.t: "And the offering of fine flour, sirs," I said, "which was prescribed to be presented on behalf of those purified from leprosy, was a type of the bread of the Eucharist, the celebration of which our Lord Jesus Christ prescribed, in remembrance of the suffering which He endured on behalf of those who are purified in soul from all iniquity, in order that we may at the same time thank God for having created the world, with all things therein, for the sake of man, and for delivering us from the evil in which we were, and for utterly overthrowing principalities and powers by Him who suffered according to His will. […]

Malachi as well contends against those of the circumcision, and speaks on behalf of the Gentiles, when he says:

"10. I have no pleasure (in you), saith the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept a sacrifice at your hands. 11. For from the rising of the sun even to the setting my name has been glorified among the Gentiles; and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering."

By "the incense and offering to be offered to God in every place,"what else can he mean, but that no longer in Jerusalem nor exclusively in that (sacred) place, but in every land and among all nations they will offer to the Supreme God the, incense of prayer and the sacrifice called "pure," because it is not a sacrifice of blood but of good works?

1:10.t: There follows: Among you the doors shall be shut, namely those of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Savior says: I am the door. Or otherwise: The doors of the Scriptures will not be opened to you, nor will you be able to look into the holy of holies, nor to know the mysteries of the Lord, nor to kindle his incense at the altar, because your prayers will not reach him. And this word which is said δωρεὰν, and which we have translated gratuitously, those who follow the understanding we are now setting out turn into grace, namely that they do not have the grace of serving the altar of the Lord.

Now I turn to Malachi. This man, prophesying of the church which by Christ's power has now expanded far and wide, takes on the person of God to say to the Jews: " 'I have no pleasure in you,' says the Lord of hosts, 'and I will not receive a gift from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to the going down thereof, my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place there is sacrifice, and there is offered to my name a clean oblation for my name is great among the Gentiles,' says the Lord of hosts." […]

1:11.t: But every Lord's day do ye gather yourselves together, and break bread, and give thanksgiving after having confessed your transgressions, that your sacrifice may be pure. But let no one that is at variance with his fellow come together with you, until they be reconciled, that your sacrifice may not be profaned. For this is that which was spoken by the Lord: In every place and time offer to me a pure sacrifice; for I am a great King, saith the Lord, and my name is wonderful among the nations.

And it is a marvel that even among us Moses is called Moses, and each of the prophets is addressed by his own name. For Christ did not change the names in them, but the understanding. And he changes it in this respect, that we should no longer attend to "Jewish fables" and "endless genealogies," because these indeed turn the hearing away from the truth, and are turned aside to fables. He opens the wells, then, and taught us that we should not seek God in any particular place, but should know that "in every land sacrifice is offered to his name." For now is that time "when the true worshipers worship the Father" neither in Jerusalem nor on Mount Gerizim, but "in spirit and in truth." Not, then, in a place nor in a land does God dwell, but he dwells in the heart. […]

And these unembodied and spiritual sacrifices the oracle of the prophet also proclaims, in a certain place:

"Offer to God the sacrifice of praise, and give the Highest thy vows: And call upon me in the day of thy affliction, and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me."

And again:

"The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice."And once more: "The sacrifice of God is a contrite spirit."

And so all these predictions of immemorial prophecy are being fulfilled at this present time through the teaching of our Saviour among all nations. Truth bears witness with the prophetic voice with which God, rejecting the Mosaic sacrifices, foretells that the future lies with us:

"Wherefore from the rising of the sun unto the setting my name shall be glorified among the nations. […]

1:11.t: By these things Israel of old, having first, as in a figure, striven for the victory, came to the feast, for these things were then foreshadowed and typified. But we, my beloved, the shadow having received its fulfilment, and the types being accomplished, should no longer consider the feast typical, neither should we go up to Jerusalem which is here below, to sacrifice the Passover, according to the unseasonable observance of the Jews, lest, while the season passes away, we should be regarded as acting unseasonably; but, in accordance with the injunction of the Apostles, let us go beyond the types, and sing the new song of praise. […]

Not therefore separately, but unitedly and collectively, let us all keep the feast together, as the prophet exhorts, saying, ‘O come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us make a joyful noise unto God our Saviour.’ Who then is so negligent, or who so disobedient to the divine voice, as not to leave everything, and run to the general and common assembly of the feast? which is not in one place only, for not one place alone keeps the feast; but ‘into all the earth their song has gone forth, and to the ends of the world their words.’ And the sacrifice is not offered in one place, but ‘in every nation, incense and a pure sacrifice is offered unto God.’ […]

He has in several ways changed the baptism ritual of the priesthood and the divine service, which was confined to one place, for instead of daily baptisms he has given only one, which is that into his death. Instead of one tribe, he has pointed out that out of every nation the best should be ordained for the priesthood; and that rather than their bodies, their religion and their lives should be examined for blemishes. Instead of a bloody sacrifice, he has appointed that reasonable and unbloody mystical one of his body and blood, which is performed to represent the death of the Lord by symbols. Instead of the divine service confined to one place, he has commanded and appointed that he should be glorified from sun rising to sun setting in every place of his dominion.

I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept a gift from your hand.

For from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made, and a clean oblation is offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts. And you have polluted it, in that you say: The table of the Lord is defiled, and what is placed upon it is contemptible, with the fire that devours it. And you have said: Behold, from toil, and you have blown upon it, says the Lord of hosts. And you have brought in from plunder the lame and the sick, and you have brought in a gift. Shall I accept it from your hand? says the Lord. […]

Some think that this, which is said specifically to the Jews, because their victims are unclean and polluted and the sacrifice is transferred to the nations, ought to be understood of the priests of the church, who offer victims to the Lord negligently. But if we accept this, then the victims must again be transferred from the Church to another religion. And as the gospel succeeded the law, so in turn things that will never be will succeed the gospel. They also refer the defiled table of the Lord to the holy Scriptures, if they are understood otherwise than as they were written.

Whether betrayers of the divine books ordained Caecilian, I do not know; I did not see; I heard it from his enemies; it's not declared to me by the law of God, or by the preaching of the prophets, or by the holy psalms, or by the apostles of Christ or by Christ's words. But the testimonies of the entire Scripture proclaim with one voice that the church, with which the sect of Donatus is not in communion, is indeed spread throughout the entire world. "In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed," said the law of God. "From the rising of the sun even to the going down, there is offered to my name a clean offering, for my name is great among the Gentiles," said God through the prophet.

You have all just now been born again of water and the spirit, and can see that food and drink upon this table of the Lord in a new light, and receive it with a fresh love and piety. So I am obliged by the duty I have of giving you a sermon and by the anxious care by which I have given you birth, that Christ might be formed in you, to remind you infants of what the meaning is of such a great and divine sacrament, such a splendid and noble medicine, such a pure and simple sacrifice, which is not offered now just in the one earthly city of Jerusalem, nor into that tabernacle which was constructed by Moses, nor in the temple built by Solomon. These were just "shadows of things to come." […]

For, from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same, my name is great among the nations; and in every place incense is offered unto my name and a pure offering, for my name is great among the nations, saith the Lord Almighty.

With bread and wine Melchisedek, the priest of the most high God, received Abraham on his return from the slaughter of the Gentiles. That table pre-imaged this mystical table, just as that priest was a type and image of Christ, the true high-priest. For thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedek. Of this bread the show-bread was an image. This surely is that pure and bloodless sacrifice which the Lord through the prophet said is offered to Him from the rising to the setting of the sun.

1:13.t: Nor is the impiety of your former speech enough, but you have also said this: Behold, from toil, and you have blown upon it, says the Lord of hosts. The sense of this speech is this: You have said: We have returned from captivity, we have been a prey to enemies, we have toiled much on a long journey, we are poor, whatever we were able to have has been consumed by the toil of the road, we offer such things as we have; and by saying these things you have blown upon your sacrifices, that is, you have made them worthy of my blowing upon them. Or, as can be read in the Hebrew: And you have blown upon me by saying these things: you have done injury not to the sacrifice but to me, to whom you were sacrificing. Wherefore I will by no means accept it from your hand, says the Lord Almighty.

1:14.t: We can take the cursed and deceitful one to be the people of the Jews, who, though they had a male in their flock, the Lord Savior, the spotless lamb who takes away the sins of the world, and though admonished by the prophecy of all the prophets to sacrifice and receive the ram that was caught by its horns in the thicket Sabec, would not do this, but sacrifices a feeble one to the Lord, crucifying the Savior and choosing Barabbas, the author of robbery and sedition, who according to the mystical senses is referred to the devil; and while they despise him and prefer the devil to the Savior, the name of Christ is dreadful among the nations, which have received the passion of the Lord and venerate him with awe-struck honor. LXX: And cursed is he who was powerful, and had a male in his flock, and his vow was upon it, and sacrifices a feeble one to the Lord, because I am a great king, says the Lord Almighty, and my name is illustrious among the nations.
