2:1.t: In which place, dearest brother, we must consider, for the sake of the faith and the religion of the sacerdotal office which we discharge, whether the account can be satisfactory in the day of judgment for a priest of God, who maintains, and approves, and acquiesces in the baptism of blasphemers, when the Lord threatens, and says, "And now, O ye priests, this commandment is for you: if ye will not hear, and if ye will not lay it to heart to give glory unto my name, saith the Lord Almighty, I will even send a curse upon you, and I will curse your blessings." Does he give glory to God, who communicates with the baptism of Marcion? Does he give glory to God, who judges that remission of sins is granted among those who blaspheme against God? […]

Hence it is said in its proper sense to the priests that, if they will not hear and keep it in their heart, so as to give glory to the name of the Lord by good conduct, but on the contrary his name is cursed among the nations because of them, he will send upon them want of all good things, and turn their blessings into a curse. Those who abuse health for lust, and turn riches into luxury, and disfigure a good reputation by sordid conduct, these change the blessings of God into a curse. […]

2:3.t: Behold, I will cast the arm at you, and I will scatter upon your face the dung of your solemnities, and it will take you with it. And you shall know that I have sent to you your commandment, that my covenant might be with Levi, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: Behold, I will separate the shoulder from you, and I will scatter the stomach upon your face, the stomach of your solemnities, and I will receive you together; and you shall know that I have sent to you this commandment, that my testament might be with the Levites, says the Lord Almighty. Since he is speaking to the priests: I will cast, he says, into your faces the things you think holier in the law, and granted to you by God from the sacrificial victims as a reward for virtues. […]

Now God willed all men indeed, but especially priests, to have no blemish, and to adorn either the shoulder or the arm with good works. In the breast a good conscience is signified; in the tongue holy confession, so that what we believe with the heart unto justice we may confess with the mouth unto salvation. In the stomach too, to have nothing deadly, but what sustains and quickens our life; for unless food is digested in the stomach, and the body is watered by its juice, the body wastes away, lacks strength, and is borne toward death. But we turn everything to the contrary, so that the Lord casts the arm at us, or separates our works from the works of the saints; […]

And it will take you, he says, with it, that is, the dung of your solemnities, so that your stinking faces may be befouled by the putrid admixture of dung; and so that, from the fact that I cast you away, you may understand that I am the very one who once chose your father Levi, and through Levi Aaron, and granted you the glory of the priesthood, that my covenant or testament might be with Levi, and he might minister to me in an eternal priesthood. It is to be noted that the Hebrew word brith Aquila translates συνθήκην, that is, covenant; the LXX always διαθήκην, that is, testament; and that in very many places of the Scriptures testament means not the will of the dead, but the covenant of the living.

And because, for what we have translated: The dung will take you with it, the Seventy translated: And I will take you up together, an interpretation is supplied: that after the priests have been covered with shame and disgrace, and have understood their sin, and have done penance, they are then taken up by the Lord; and that what follows fits this sense: And you shall know that I have sent this commandment to you. But the former interpretation seems to me the true one, lest among words of threatening he should have placed the words of one who coaxes, especially since what follows also speaks of the indignation of God.

2:5.t: Again he reminds them of the covenant of God, a covenant of life and peace, with the sons of Levi, and that they should serve Him in fear, and stand in awe of the manifestation of His Name. The law of truth, he says, was in his mouth, and unrighteousness was not found in his lips; he walked with me uprightly in peace, and turned away many from iniquity: for the priest's lips shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth. And how honourable and at the same time how fearful is the cause! for he is the messenger of the Lord Almighty. Although I pass over the following imprecations, as strongly worded, yet I am afraid of their truth.

My covenant with him was of life and peace, and I gave him fear, and he feared me, and he trembled before the face of my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips; in peace and in equity he walked with me, and he turned many away from iniquity. For the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts. LXX: My testament with him was of life and peace, and I gave him fear, that he might fear me and be afraid before the face of my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips. In peace, directing, he walked with me, and he converted many from iniquity. […]

A little further on Malachi speaks of Christ, again in the person of God: "My covenant was with him of life and peace, and I gave him fear; and he feared me, and he was afraid before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips. He walked with me in peace and equity and turned many away from iniquity. For the lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the laws at his mouth because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts." No one should be astonished to hear Christ spoken of as "the angel of the Lord of hosts." He was called his servant because he came to humanity in the form of a servant; similarly he was called an angel because of the evangel, which he brought to humankind.

2:6.t: The law of truth was in his mouth, that is, the teaching of the apostles, which in a priest ought to be disfigured by no poisoning, but should proceed wholly from the fountain of truth. And iniquity was not found on his lips, so that he may imitate his Lord, of whom it is said: Who did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. In peace and in equity he walked with me, so that he may both have peace in himself and make peace for others, and accept no one's person in judgement, and therefore walk with God, as Enoch walked, who was translated to the Lord and was not found: And he turned many away from iniquity. He who is a priest, and does not rebuke those who offend, passes over the office of a priest.

2:7.t: And as to what the apostles say, that We shall judge angels, hear, and I will instruct thee. The angels who shall be judged by the apostles are the priests who have violated the law; as the Prophet said, The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and the law shall they inquire of his mouth; because he is the angel of the Lord, the most mighty. The angels who are the priests, of whose mouth the law is inquired, when they transgress the law, shall be judged at the last by the apostles, and the priests who observe the law.
2:7.s: Demonstration 22 (Of Death and the Latter Times), Section 16

2:7.t: For neither may we address ourselves to almighty God, but only by Christ. In the same manner, therefore, let the laity make known all their desires to the bishop by the deacon, and accordingly let them act as he shall direct them. For there was no holy thing offered or done in the temple formerly without the priest. "For the priest's lips shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth," as the prophet somewhere says, "for he is the messenger of the Lord God almighty."

The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge; he did not say, shall bring forth, but, shall keep, so that they may speak in season, and give their fellow servants their food in due season. And they shall seek the law from his mouth. In Haggai the same is written: Ask the priests the law of the Lord. It belongs to the discipline of a priest, when asked, to answer concerning the law. If, diligent in other matters, he pleads an ignorance that is negligent in the holy Scriptures, he boasts in vain of a dignity whose works he does not display. This is what the apostle Paul writes to Titus: That he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine, and to refute those who contradict. […]

For in sacred language teachers are sometimes called prophets, in that, by pointing out how fleeting are present things, they make manifest the things that are to come. And such the divine discourse convinces of seeing false things, because, while fearing to reprove faults, they vainly flatter evil doers by promising security: neither do they at all discover the iniquity of sinners, since they refrain their voice from chiding. For the language of reproof is the key of discovery, because by chiding it discloses the fault of which even he who has committed it is often himself unaware. Hence Paul says, "That he may be able by sound doctrine even to convince the gainsayers." Hence through Malachi it is said, "The priest's lips keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth." […]
2:7.s: The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 2, Chapter 4

2:8.t: But you have departed from the way, and have made very many stumble in the law; you have made void the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of hosts. Wherefore I too have made you contemptible and lowly to all peoples, as you have not kept my ways, and have accepted the face in the law. LXX: But you have turned aside from my way, and have made many weak in the law; you have corrupted the testament of Levi, says the Lord Almighty. And I have made you contemptible and dissolute among all the nations, because you have not guarded my ways, but accepted persons in the law. That these things do not pertain to the person of Christ, nor to those who are dedicated to his worship, the prudent reader understands even if I am silent. […]

2:9.t: For which reason I too, he says, have made you contemptible and lowly to all peoples, so that they might despise you, and instead of honor and glory trample on you as cast down and lowly: As you have not kept my ways, and have accepted the face in the law. Among all the sins of Levi, or of those who are from Levi, the priests of God, this one is set down as both the last and the greatest: that they accept the face in the law, so that they consider not causes but persons, and, despising the just poor man, receive and honor the unjust rich. To them it is said in Psalm 81 (82): How long do you judge iniquity, and take up the faces of sinners? And Paul to the Galatians: God, he says, does not accept the person of man. And the apostle James rebukes and condemns this sin more fully. […]

2:10.t: Truly, then, the Scripture declared, which says, "First of all believe that there is one God, who has established all things, and completed them, and having caused that from what had no being, all things should come into existence:" He who contains all things, and is Himself contained by no one. Rightly also has Malachi said among the prophets: "Is it not one God who hath established us? Have we not all one Father?" In accordance with this, too, does the apostle say, "There is one God, the Father, who is above all, and in us all." Likewise does the Lord also say: "All things are delivered to Me by My Father;" manifestly by Him who made all things; for He did not deliver to Him the things of another, but His own. […]

They shall not marry wives there, nor shall they beget children; nor shall there the male be distinguished from the female; but all shall be sons of their Father Who is in heaven; as the Prophet said:—Is there not one Father of us all; is there not one God Who created us?
2:10.s: Demonstration 22 (Of Death and the Latter Times), Section 12

2:10.t: But this is God's kindness to humanity, that of whom he is the maker, of them according to grace he afterwards becomes Father also. He becomes, that is, when people, his creatures, receive him into their hearts, as the apostle says, "the spirit of his Son, crying, 'Abba, Father.' " And these are they who, having received the word, gained power from him to become sons of God; for they could not become sons, being by nature creatures, otherwise than by receiving the spirit of the natural and true Son. Wherefore, that this might be, "the word became flesh," that he might make humans capable of godhood. This same meaning may be gained from the prophet Malachi, who says, "Has not one God created us? Have we not all one Father?" […]

Is not one Father of us all? Has not one God created us? Why then does each one of us despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers? Judah has transgressed, and abomination has been done in Israel and in Jerusalem, because Judah has defiled the sanctification of the Lord, which he loved, and has had the daughter of a strange god. May the Lord destroy the man who shall have done this, the master and the disciple, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him who offers a gift to the Lord of hosts. LXX: Is not one Father of us all? Has not one God created us? Why has each one forsaken his brother, so as to make abominable the testament of your fathers? […]

Some, not understanding this place, nor knowing the truth of the history, understand what he says, Is not one father of us all?, of Abraham in such a way that they recall that Abraham is the father of the nations too, according to what is written: Is God able from these stones to raise up sons to Abraham? Or at any rate they affirm one God the Father, according to what we read in Deuteronomy: Is not this the very Father who possessed you, and made you, and created you? And again: You have forsaken the God who created you. And elsewhere: I have begotten sons and exalted them: but they have forsaken me. And in the volume of the psalms: Strange sons have lied to me, strange sons have grown old and have gone lame from their paths. […]

2:11.t: And if you wish to see more clearly how utterly unlawful it is for a Christian woman to marry a Gentile, consider what the same apostle says, "A wife is bound for so long time as her husband lives. But if the husband be dead, she is freed to be married to whom she will, only in the Lord," that is, to a Christian. The one who allows second and third marriages in the Lord forbids first marriages with a Gentile. Whence Abraham also makes his servant swear upon his thigh, that is, on Christ, who was to spring from his seed, that he would not bring an alien-born as a wife for his son Isaac. And Ezra checked an offense of this kind against God by making his countrymen put away their wives. […]

Judah has transgressed; for this tribe returned from Babylon with the priests and Levites; and abomination has been done in Israel and in Jerusalem. Not at all among the ten tribes, which were held by the Assyrians, but among those which returned from Babylon by command of King Cyrus under Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah. Because Judah has defiled the sanctification of the Lord, which he loved, and has had the daughter of a strange god, by mingling with foreigners the seed of Israel and of the Gentiles; that is, by taking as wives the daughters of the heathen, who serve idols. Since, therefore, they have done this, the word of the prophet is directed to them, and they are drawn back from sin by curses.

In short, what follows according to the LXX, Judah has been forsaken, and abomination has been done in Israel, and in Jerusalem, they expound thus: that the Jews have been forsaken because they blasphemed the Lord Savior, and have suffered what is written: According to the multitude of their impieties drive them out, for they have provoked you, O Lord, so that they were scattered as wanderers and fugitives through all the provinces. For they defiled the holy things of the Lord, loving, in place of the Son of God, and devising for themselves, strange gods: For he who does not receive the Son does not receive the Father, who sent him. […]

2:12.t: May the Lord destroy the man who shall have done this. How beautifully he does not cut off pardon from error, nor did he say, May the Lord curse him who has done this, but, who shall have done, stretching the curse into the future, so as to call sinners to repentance. The teacher, he says, and the disciple, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, whether he be a priest or a layman, will be struck by one curse, and there will be no difference of punishment among those in whom the sins are equal. And him who offers a gift to the Lord of hosts: it is understood, may the Lord destroy him also who would wish to offer a gift at the altar for men of this kind, whose only remedy is not to do what they have done.

2:13.t: What we have expounded specially, according to the book of Ezra, concerning the forsaken wives, others think is said generally against those who plunder what belongs to others and, gathering riches unjustly, dare to offer gifts to God, which he says he can by no means accept, prevented by the tears and weeping and groans of those who have been laid waste; and that this place agrees with that testimony: Honor God from your just labors. But they also insert this sense: that those who, because of the loss of their property, and the death of their children, and shipwreck, and the other things that belong to the loss of worldly goods, are turned to weeping and give themselves wholly to lamentation and groaning, and do not, by strength of mind and hope in God and the rewards of things to […]

And this again you have done: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping and groaning, so that I no longer look upon sacrifice, nor accept anything pleasing from your hand. And you have said: For what reason? Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your puberty, whom you have despised; and she is your partner and the wife of your compact. Did not one make, and is the remnant of the spirit his? And what does the one seek, but the seed of God? Guard therefore your spirit; and do not despise the wife of your youth. Since you have hated, put away, says the Lord God of Israel; but iniquity shall cover his garment, says the Lord of hosts. Guard your spirit, and do not despise. […]

2:14.t: Now what follows, Because the Lord has borne witness between you and the wife of your puberty, or of your youth, whom you have despised; and she is your partner and the wife of your covenant, or of your testament, ; and no other made her: and the remnant of your spirit, they interpret thus, so as to call the wife of youth the natural understanding and the law written in the heart, which is implanted in all men. Whence also the nations, not having the law of God, do the things that are of the law. Of this spouse, they say, it is proclaimed in Proverbs: A wife is joined to a man by God; and we are commanded to drink from our own waters and fountains, and that no one be partner in the drinking, and that we rejoice with the wife of our youth. […]

2:15.t: For in the Gospel of Matthew he says, "Whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causes her to commit adultery." He also is deemed equally guilty of adultery who marries a woman put away by her husband. The Creator, however, except on account of adultery, does not put asunder that which he himself joined together, the same Moses in another passage enacting that he who had married after violence to a damsel should thenceforth not have it in his power to put away his wife. Now if a compulsory marriage contracted after violence shall be permanent, how much rather shall a voluntary one, the result of an agreement! This has the sanction of the prophet: "You shall not forsake the wife of your youth." […]

And the remnant of his spirit, whether of God, as some think, or of the husband, as others suppose, because through affection one soul seems in a certain manner to be in two, joined in spirit, united in mind. Since, then, one made both, both the man and the woman, the union of both was therefore made by the Lord, that children might be born. For the one God, what does he seek but the seed of God, that is, sons begotten of the Israelite stock? Since, then, you have fruitful wives and rejoice in children, why do you seek beauty in wives, which is fitting for harlots, not for wives? So God commands through the prophet, and says: Guard your spirit, that you be not led away by lust, that you be not overcome by love of foreign women. […]

This wife is the remnant of our spirit, because she is always joined to our sense; and if she withdraws from us, at once we offend God, and our impiety covers us. Hence again it is urged: Guard your spirit; not the flesh, for those who are in it cannot please God; not the soul: The natural for man does not receive the things that are of the spirit; but the spirit: Because the spirit intercedes for us with unutterable groanings.

2:16.t: But it could happen that the princes, priests, Levites and people would answer: God commanded through Moses that when we have hated our wives, we should put them away. And it is to be read: You tell me, it is written: Since you have hated, put away your wife, says the Lord God of Israel. And at once he answered: This was indeed commanded in the law, but because of the hardness of your heart. Which the Lord pursues more fully in the Gospel: But whoever, except for the cause of fornication, unjustly puts away his wife, iniquity shall cover his garment, that is, the body with which the soul is clothed, says the Lord of hosts, so that he may be punished in that very thing in which he sinned. […]

2:17.t: You have made the Lord labor with your words, and you have said: In what have we made him labor? In this, that you say: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such please him; or at any rate, where is the God of judgement? LXX: You who have provoked the Lord with your words, and you have said: In what have we provoked him? In this, that you say: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and in these he is well pleased; and where is the God of justice? This passage is pursued more fully by Psalm 72 (73), whose beginning is: How good is the God of Israel to those who are of right heart. But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well-nigh been poured out. For I was jealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners. […]

Wherefore now we call the proud people happy, for they that work wickedness are built up. It was such complaints as these that compelled the prophet to anticipate, as it were, the last judgment in which the wicked will be so far from even a pretense of happiness that their misery will be apparent to all, whereas the good, untroubled by even transitory sorrow, will enjoy a manifest and unending blessedness. Malachi had already given a similar illustration of the kind of murmurings that wearied the Lord: "Everyone who does evil is [thought to be] good in the sight of the Lord and as such pleases him." The only point I want to make is that such murmurings against God were the result of an unspiritual interpretation of the law.

3:1.t: And that we may not have to ask, Of what God was the Word made flesh? he does himself previously teach us, saying, "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. The same came as a witness, that he might bear witness of that Light. He was not that Light, but [came] that he might testify of the Light." By what God, then, was John, the forerunner, who testifies of the Light, sent [into the world]? Truly it was by Him, of whom Gabriel is the angel, who also announced the glad tidings of his birth: [that God] who also had promised by the prophets that He would send His messenger before the face of His Son, who should prepare His way, that is, that he should bear witness of that Light in the spirit and power of Elias. But, again, of what God was Elias the servant and the prophet? […]

Someone else will appeal to the text, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness," and maintain that whatever is made according to God's image and likeness is man. To support this, numberless instances are adduced to show that in Scripture "man" and "angel" are used indifferently and that the same subject is called both angel and man. This is true of the three who were entertained by Abraham and of the two who came to Sodom. In the whole course of Scripture, persons are styled sometimes men, sometimes angels. […]
3:1.s: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 2:17

3:1.t: John, however, as soon as he was born, passed over to the deserts, and he who "was greater among those born of women" showed himself worthy of a greater nurture. Of him the prophet speaks: "behold, I send my angel before your face". Rightly is he called an angel, who had been sent before the Lord and, as soon as he was born, was able to hear and understand his prophesying father.
3:1.s: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

3:1.t:
[Passage quoted, Mal. iii. 1-2.]

THIS, too, is like the former prophecies. For the Lord God Himself, the Almighty, says that a Lord will come in His own temple, speaking of another: And He surely means God the Word. And after this also He names Him "the Angel of the Covenant" of Whom, too, Almighty God teaches that He will Him send forth before His face, saying, "Behold, I send forth my angel before my face." And this same Being, Whom He has called "My angel," He calls Lord directly after, and adds, "The Lord shall suddenly come, and the Angel of the Covenant." Thus having referred to one and the same Being, He proceeds, "Behold he comes, and who will abide the day of his coming?" meaning His Second and Glorious Coming. […]
3:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 28

3:1.t: WHAT DOES THIS MEAN, THAT ALTHOUGH IT IS WRITTEN IN THE PROPHET MALACHI, “BEHOLD, I SEND MY ANGEL BEFORE YOUR FACE, WHO WILL PREPARE YOUR WAY BEFORE YOU,” THE EVANGELIST MARK CLAIMS THAT THIS IS WRITTEN IN THE PROPHET ISAIAH (Mal. 3:1; Mark 1:2)? — Mark could not have been unaware of what he was writing; for he was not lacking in learning, since from childhood he had been immersed in the divine Scriptures and trained in the Law, especially as he had followed the Apostles. Knowing that all sayings must be referred back to their original author, he attributed these words to Isaiah, who had first conveyed this meaning when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40:3). […]
3:1.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 57: WHY MARK ATTRIBUTES MALACHI'S WORDS TO ISAIAH

3:1.t: Of these two comings the prophet Malachi says, "And suddenly there will come to the temple the Lord whom you seek"; that is one coming. Of the second coming he says, " 'And the messenger of the covenant whom you desire, yes, he is coming,' says the Lord of hosts. 'But who will endure the day of his coming? And who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire or like the fuller's lye. He will sit refining and purifying.' " In what immediately follows the Savior himself says, "I will draw near to you for judgment, and I will be swift to bear witness against sorcerers, adulterers and perjurers." […]

And what sort of connexion may this have with what was said before? Much, assuredly, and in full accordance therewith. Yea, by this topic also He proceeds to urge and press them into the faith of Himself; and at the same time likewise, He is speaking in agreement with what had been before said by John. "For if all things are fulfilled even down to John, I am "He that should come." For all the prophets," saith He, "and the law prophesied until John." For the prophets would not have ceased, unless I were come. Expect therefore nothing further, neither wait for any one else. For that I am He is manifest both from the prophets ceasing, and from those that every day "take by force" the faith that is in me. For so manifest is it and certain, that many even take it by force. […]
3:1.s: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 37

3:1.t: Behold, I send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face; and at once the Ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the testament whom you desire. LXX: Behold, I will send my angel, and he will prepare the way before my face; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of justice whom you desire. The Lord in the Gospel interpreted this of John the Baptist, saying: This is he of whom it is written: Behold, I will send my angel before your face, and he will prepare your way before me; nor did he use the same words which the LXX translators rendered. […]

Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts.

And who will be able to think of the day of his coming? And who will stand to see him? For he is like a refining fire, and like fullers' herb. And he will sit refining and cleansing as silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and will strain them like gold and like silver, and they will be offering sacrifices to the Lord in justice. And the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please the Lord, as the days of the age, and as the ancient years. And I will draw near to you in judgement, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers and adulterers, and perjurers, and those who wrong the hireling over his wages, the widows and orphans, and oppress the stranger, and have not feared me, says the Lord of hosts. […]

For this is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah, saying: The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. He was preparing the souls of believers, in which the Lord was going to walk, so that he, the pure one, might walk in most pure ways, saying: I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Porphyry compares this passage with the beginning of the evangelist Mark, in which it is written: The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; as it is written in the prophet Isaiah: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way; the voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. […]

And because to the prophetic privilege there was added also the Baptist's reward, that he should baptize his own Lord, he therefore brings in an αὔξησιν (increase) of his merits, producing the testimony from Malachi in which he is even proclaimed an angel. But let us not think that John is called an angel here by a sharing of nature, but by the dignity of his office, that is, a messenger, because he announced the Lord who was to come.

Speaking further of Christ in the same vein, Malachi says, "Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face. And presently the Lord, whom you seek, and the angel of the testament whom you desire, shall come into the temple. Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts. And who shall be able to think of the day of his coming? And who shall stand to see him?" In this text he foretells both comings of Christ, the first and the second—the first where he says, "And presently the Lord shall come into his temple." This refers to Christ's body, of which he himself said in the Gospel, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." His second coming is foretold in these words: " 'Behold, he comes,' says the Lord of hosts. […]

It is the custom moreover of the divinely inspired Scripture to give the name of fire sometimes to the divine and sacred words, and to the efficacy and power which is by the Holy Spirit, and whereby we are made, as I said, "fervent in spirit." For one of the holy prophets thus spoke as in the person of God respecting Christ our common Saviour: "The Lord, Whom you seek, shall suddenly come to His temple, even the Messenger of the covenant, Whom you desire: behold He comes, says the Lord. And who shall endure the day of His coming? or who shall stand at the sight of Him? For lo! He comes like the fire of a furnace, and like the sulphur of the bleacher. And He shall sit, like one that smelts and purifies as silver and as gold." […]
3:1.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

3:1.t: Behold I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before thy presence. This passage the Lord applied to himself and to John the Baptist.

3:2.t: But as it is in mockery that Celsus says we speak of "God coming down like a torturer bearing fire" and thus compels us unseasonably to investigate words of deeper meaning, we shall make a few remarks, sufficient to enable our hearers to form an idea of the defense which disposes of the ridicule of Celsus against us. And then we shall turn to what follows. The divine word says that our God is "a consuming fire" and that "he draws rivers of fire before him." He even enters in as "a refiner's fire and as a fuller's herb," to purify his own people. But when he is said to be a "consuming fire," we inquire what are the things that are appropriate to be consumed by God. […]

And who will be able to think of the day of his coming? If no one can think of it, because of the power of his majesty, who will be able to bear it? And who will stand to see him, that is, who will be able with bleary and half-blind eyes to look upon him in his brightness, who is the Sun of justice, and in whose wings is healing? He will come like a refining fire, and like fullers' herb. Fire for shall burn before him, and round about him a mighty tempest. Then he will call the heaven from above, and the earth, that he may judge his people; rivers of fire will flow before him, rolling along every sinner. Now the Lord is called fire, and a consuming fire, that he may burn up our wood, hay and stubble. […]

3:3.t: And he will sit refining and cleansing as silver, so that, according to Ezekiel, whatever bronze, tin, iron and lead has been mixed into our gold and silver, that is, into our sense and our speech, may be thoroughly smelted in the furnace of the Lord, so that pure gold and silver may remain. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: I came to send fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it may burn, and he will purify the sons of Levi. For it is time that judgement begin from the house of God. And elsewhere it is written: Begin from my holy ones. In the sons of Levi, understand the whole priestly dignity. But if the priests must be purified and strained, so that pure gold and silver may remain, what is to be said of the rest?

When they have been cleansed and strained, then they will offer just sacrifices to the Lord, and their sacrifice will please, which they offer for Judah and Jerusalem, that is, for those who confess the Lord and behold his peace with the mind, as the days of the age, and as the ancient years, so that as in the beginning they pleased God, so after sin and repentance they may begin to please, when they have been purged of every filth of sins.

3:5.t: And I will draw near, he says, to you in judgement, and I will be a swift witness. How great is the dread of the judgement, since he himself is both witness and judge. And he is a witness against all sorcerers and adulterers, for these crimes are committed in secret, and therefore they are brought out into the open, lest they lie hidden long. After the sorcerers are placed the adulterers, after the adulterers the perjurers, after the perjurers those who wrong the hireling over his wages and will not pay what they owe for the labor of the work. Widows also and orphans they wrong, as is understood; and they oppress the stranger and the foreigner, or at any rate the catechumen, who has not yet been made a citizen in the city of Christ. […]

3:6.t: But let us look at what Celsus next with ostentation announces in the following fashion: "And again," he says, "let us resume the subject from the beginning, with a larger array of proofs. And I make no new proofs. And I make no new statement but say what has long been settled. God is good and beautiful and blessed, and that in the best and most beautiful degree. But if he comes down among humanity, he must undergo a change, and a change from good to evil, from virtue to vice, from happiness to misery, and from best to worst. Who, then, would make a choice of such a change? It is the nature of a mortal, indeed, to undergo change and remolding, but of an immortal to remain the same and unaltered. God, then, could not admit such a change." […]

He, then, is always like to Himself; nor does He ever turn or change Himself into any forms, lest by change He should appear to be mortal. For the change implied in turning from one thing to another is comprehended as a portion of a certain death. Thus there is never in Him any accession or increase of any part or honour, lest anything should appear to have ever been wanting to His perfection, nor is any loss sustained in Him, lest a degree of mortality should appear to have been suffered by Him. But what He is, He always is; and who He is, He is always Himself; and what character He has, He always has. For increasing argues beginning, as well as losses prove death and perishing. And therefore He says, "I am God, I change not;" […]

He does not lack things that are of Him and through Him and in Him. The Source and Maker of all, Who contains all, Who is beyond all, does not need that which is within Him, the Creator His creatures, the Possessor His possessions. Nothing is prior to Him, nothing derived from any other than Him, nothing beyond Him. What element of fulness is still lacking in God, which time will supply to make Him all in all? Whence can He receive it, if outside Him is nothing, and while nothing is outside Him, He is eternally Himself? And if He is eternally Himself, and there is nothing outside Him, with what increase shall He be made full, by what addition shall He be made other than He is? Did He not say, I am and I change not? What possibility is there of change in Him? […]

I am told that there are some who are endeavouring to deprave the right doctrine of the Lord’s incarnation by perverse opinions, and I therefore call upon them through you to hold off from those unreasonable views, which some are reported to me to hold. I mean that God Himself was turned into flesh; that He did not assume, through the Holy Mary, the nature of Adam, but, in His own proper Godhead, was changed into a material nature.

This absurd position can be easily confuted. The blasphemy is its own conviction, and I therefore think that, for one who fears the Lord, the mere reminder is enough. If He was turned, then He was changed. But far be it from me to say or think such a thing, when God has declared, “I am the Lord, I change not.” […]

And what follows, I am the Lord and I do not change, he sets down for this reason, because he had said above, He is like a refining fire, and like fullers' herb, lest we should think that he changes the nature of his divinity when for our sake he is named either angel, or fire, or borith.

And you, sons of Jacob, have not been consumed.

For from the days of your fathers you have departed from my ordinances, and have not kept them. LXX: And you, sons of Jacob, have not departed from the sins of your fathers; you have turned aside from my ordinances, and have not kept them. He had said above: I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers and the adulterers and the perjurers, and those who wrong the hireling over his wages, the widows and the orphans, and oppress the stranger and have not feared me, says the Lord of hosts. And saying that he is a just judge, in that he does not accept persons in judgement, he added: I am the Lord, and I do not change. […]

Wherefore it will be a clear proof of our failure if we find that we have gained nothing more, nor should we doubt but that we have altogether gone back, whenever we find that we have not advanced upwards, because, as I said, the mind of man cannot possibly continue in the same condition, nor so long as he is in the flesh will any of the saints ever reach the height of all virtues, so that they continue unalterable. For something must either be added to them or taken away from them, and in no creature can there be such perfection, as not to be subject to the feeling of change; as we read in the book of Job: "What is man that he should be without spot, and he that is born of a woman that he should appear just? […]

That the divine being is immutable is shown thus: First, by authority, Malachi 3: I am God and I do not change: the Gloss says: "He says this lest it be thought that there is any mutability in God."

It must be said that without doubt the divine being is altogether immutable: and this indeed must be maintained, although we cannot perfectly understand it; whence all agree in maintaining it. For all who rightly understand, not only the Saints but also the philosophers, maintain that the divine being is immutable, because it is most simple, immense, and eternal. […]
3:6.s: Quaestiones Disputatae, De Mysterio Trinitatis, Question 6

3:7.t: And while God is provoked with frequent and continual offenses, he softens his indignation, and in his patience waits for the day of retribution, once for all determined. And although he has revenge in his power, he prefers to keep patience for a long while. [He bears], that is to say, mercifully, and puts off, so that, if it might be possible, the long-protracted mischief may at some time be changed, and humanity, involved in the contagion of errors and crimes, may even though late be converted to God, as he himself warns and says, "I do not will the death of him that dies, so much as that he may return and live." And again, " 'Return unto me,' says the Lord."
3:7.s: Treatise IX. On the Advantage of Patience 9:4

3:7.t: We have heard the history of Ezra; now let us take up again the words of the prophet, looking more carefully whether prophecy and history agree. When it is said: Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord Almighty, it is clear that those whom he exhorts to come back had departed from the Lord. And see the mercy of the Lord: he promises like for like, that with the measure they have measured, it may be measured back to them. And just as it is written in Leviticus: If you walk perversely towards me, I too will walk against you with perverse fury, so now too he exhorts the people to return, so that he himself also may return to them. They, not understanding that they have departed from the Lord, shamelessly ask: In what shall we return? […]

3:8.t: The Lord answered: Will a man fix God, since you fix me? The Hebrew word that is written haiecba the LXX translated 'if he supplants', in place of which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion put 'if he defrauds', so that the sense is: Does a man defraud God, since you defraud me? And indeed, according to the order of the history, because the people were not rendering the tithes and the first fruits to the Levites, the Lord says that he himself suffers fraud, since his ministers, compelled by famine and want, had deserted the temple. For if it is he who is visited in prison through others, and taken in when sick, and receives food and is given drink when hungry and thirsty, why should he himself not receive tithes in his ministers; […]

What we have said of the tithes and first fruits, which were once given by the people to the priests and Levites, understand also of the peoples of the Church, who have been commanded not only to give tithes and first fruits, but also to sell all that they have and give to the poor and follow the Lord and Savior. But if we are unwilling to do this, let us at least imitate the beginnings of the Jews, so that we give to the poor a part of the whole, and pay due honour to the priests and Levites. Hence the Apostle too says: Honour widows who are widows indeed; and that the presbyter is to be honoured with double honour, especially he who labours in the word and in the teaching of God. […]

Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord of hosts. And you have said: In what shall we return?

Will a man fix God, since you fix me? And you have said: In what have we fixed you? In tithes and in first fruits. In want you are cursed, and you have fixed me, the whole nation. Bring every tithe into the storehouse, and let there be food in my house, and prove me in this, says the Lord: if I do not open to you the floodgates of heaven, and pour out on you a blessing even to abundance. And I will rebuke for your sake the devourer, and he will not spoil the fruit of your vine, nor will the vine in the field be barren, says the Lord of hosts. And all the nations will call you blessed; for you will be a desirable land, says the Lord of hosts. […]

We can also interpret the tithes and first fruits thus: If someone learned and instructed in the law of God is able to instruct others, he ought not to attribute it to his own prudence and to the talent that he possesses; but let him give thanks first to God, who bestows all things, then to his priests and teachers, by whom he was taught. For if he does not give thanks, but claims knowledge for himself, he will be cursed in want. But if, understanding God to be the giver, and giving thanks to those through whom he was instructed by God, he humbles himself and brings food into the storehouse of God, that is, ministers the nourishment of holy Scripture to the peoples in the Church, at once the floodgates of heaven will be opened over him, and spiritual rain will be poured out; […]

3:9.t: Because you have not rendered to me the tithes and first fruits, therefore you are cursed in famine and want, and you supplant me, or defraud and deprive me, the whole nation. For 'nation', which in the Hebrew is written aggoi, the Seventy translated 'year', ἔτος instead of ἔθνος. And the sense is: Behold, the year is completed, and you have carried nothing into my treasuries, but everything into your own storehouses. And for the sake of tithes and first fruits, which were small things if they had been given by you, you have lost the richness of your possessions and all abundance of produce.

3:10.t: But so that you may know that this was brought about by my anger, because you defrauded me of my share, I exhort you and admonish you to bring the tithes into the storehouses, that is, into the treasuries of the temple, and let the priests and Levites who minister to me have food; and prove me, whether I do not pour out such great rains that the floodgates of heaven will be believed to have been opened. And I will pour out on you a blessing even to abundance. The word 'pouring out' shows the name of bounty.

3:11.t: But it can happen that, with rains watering the fields, there is indeed fertility; but either the locust comes, or the cankerworm, or blight, or the caterpillar, and the labours of men perish; therefore he joins to it and says: And I will rebuke for your sake the devourer, the locust, that is, and the rest that we have mentioned: And he will not spoil the fruit of your land. The vine also will fill the winepresses, and all the nations round about will marvel at the fertility of your land, so much so that all will long to dwell in it, and you will be an example to all nations of abundance in all things.

3:13.t: Hence the prophet, who is a spiritual physician, heals all the wounds, and solemnly declares that the words of blasphemy fall back upon the Creator, and he says in the person of God: Your words have grown strong against me, or have been made heavy; for indeed, according to Zechariah, iniquity sits upon a talent of lead, and what is said against God is weighed down by the heavy mass of blasphemies. They, not understanding their most grievous words and their blasphemy, ask, what have we spoken against you?

Your words have grown strong against me, says the Lord, and you have said: What have we spoken against you? You have said: Vain is he who serves God, and what profit is it that we have kept his commandments, and that we have walked sorrowful before the Lord of hosts? So now we call the arrogant blessed, since those who work impiety have been built up, and they have tempted God, and have been saved. LXX: You have made your words heavy against me, says the Lord. And you have said: In what have we spoken against you? And you have said: Vain is he who serves God; and what more. Because we have kept his commands, and because we have walked as suppliants before the face of the Lord Almighty? […]

Those who are spiritually immature put much stock in temporal promises and serve God with an eye to such remunerations. Then, when the people of evil life prosper, they are very much upset. For their enlightenment, Malachi goes on to differentiate the eternal blessedness of the New Testament, which only the good shall win, from the purely earthly good fortune of the old that as often as not comes to the wicked. He says, " 'Your words have been insufferable to me,' says the Lord. And you have said, 'What have we spoken against you?' You have said, 'He labors in vain that serves God, and what profit is it that we have kept ordinances and that we have walked sorrowfully before the Lord of hosts?' […]

3:14.t: To them the Lord answered: You have said: Vain is he who serves God, and what profit is it that we have kept his commandments? In the present age they demand a wage for the service of God; therefore they do not receive it. And that we have walked sorrowful before the Lord, according to that which is written in the psalms: All the day long I went about sorrowful; therefore we call the arrogant blessed, who are proud against God and hurl impious words of blasphemies. Since they have been built up, and after their crimes and blasphemies enjoy all prosperity, they have tempted God, or resisted God, and have been saved. They think that salvation is the happiness of the present age. And for that reason they are deceived by errors. […]

It was, in fact, of their purely material interpretation of the law and of their failure to perceive that its temporal promises were but symbols of eternal rewards that they broke into such rebellious resentfulness as to say, "He labors in vain that serves God, and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinances and that we have walked sorrowfully before the Lord of hosts? Wherefore now we call the proud people happy, for they that work wickedness are built up." It was such complaints as these that compelled the prophet to anticipate, as it were, the last judgment in which the wicked will be so far from even a pretense of happiness that their misery will be apparent to all, whereas the good, untroubled by even transitory sorrow, will enjoy a manifest and unending beatitude. […]

3:16.t: But by us, who are servants of God, who renounce both voluptuousness and ambition, each is to be repudiated. Fleshly concupiscence claims the functions of adult age, craves after beauty's harvest, rejoices in its own shame, pleads the necessity of a husband to the female sex as a source of authority and comfort or to render it safe from evil rumors. To meet these counsels, do you apply the examples of sisters of ours whose names are with the Lord—who, when their husbands have preceded them [to glory], give to no opportunity of beauty or of age the precedence over holiness. They prefer to be wedded to God. To God their beauty, to God their youth [is dedicated].

Then those who feared God spoke, each one with his neighbour. LXX: These things those who fear the Lord spoke, each one to his neighbour. According to the Hebrews it is to be understood thus: while those men were blaspheming about the judgement of God, those who fear God spoke to one another, saying that the recompense of the good or the evil is not in the present and brief age, but in the future and eternal one; and that man cannot know the judgements of God, and dispute about his equity and justice, and the other things that a just man ought to speak with a just man. […]

And the Lord attended and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the Lord, and think upon his name.

And they shall be mine, says the Lord of hosts, on the day that I make, for a special possession, and I will spare them, as a man spares his son who serves him. And you shall turn, and you shall see what difference there is between the just and the impious, and between him who serves God and him who does not serve him. LXX: And the Lord attended and heard; and he wrote a book of remembrance in his sight for those who fear the Lord, and who revere his name. And they shall be mine, says the Lord Almighty, on the day that I make, for an acquisition, and I will choose them as a man chooses his son who serves him; […]

3:17.t: And those who fear the Lord shall be to the Lord of hosts for a special possession, on the day when the time of judgement arrives. For 'special possession' in the Hebrew is read sgolla, which Aquila translated περιούσιον (special), and the others περιποίησιν (possession). Those, therefore, who fear the Lord, who spoke with their neighbour and answered the words of blasphemy, will be on the day of judgement for a special possession, and he will spare them, because every man is under sin. Or else he will choose them, as a man is wont to choose his son who serves him. In this there is a twofold affection, both of fatherly love toward a son and of service toward a servant.

3:18.t: And then you who now blaspheme and say: What profit is it that we have kept his commandments, and have walked sorrowful before the Lord? will recognize your own misery too from their election and blessedness, and, turned to repentance, you will see what difference there is between the just and the impious, and between him who serves God and him who does not serve him.

4:1.t: For behold, the day will come, kindled like a furnace; and all the proud and all who work impiety will be stubble; and the coming day will set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts, which will not leave them root and shoot. And for you who fear my name the Sun of justice will rise, and healing in his wings; and you will go forth, and leap like calves from the herd. And you will tread down the impious when they are ash under the soles of your feet, on the day that I make, says the Lord of hosts. LXX: For behold, the day comes burning like an oven, and it will burn them up; and all the foreigners, and all who work iniquity, will be stubble; the coming day will set them on fire, says the Lord Almighty, and neither root nor branch will be left in them. […]

4:2.t: But that he "sprinkles toward the east", do not take it idly. From the east atonement comes to you; for thence is the man whose "name is East", who was made "the mediator of God and men". You are invited therefore by this always to look "toward the east", whence rises for you the "sun of righteousness", whence light is born for you; so that you may never "walk in darkness" nor that last day catch you in darkness; lest the night and gloom of ignorance steal upon you, but that you may always dwell in the light of knowledge, always have the day of faith, always obtain the light of charity and peace.

[Passage quoted, Mal. iv. 2.]

HE that has often been named Lord, and God, and Angel, and Chief Captain, Christ and Priest, and Word and Wisdom of God, and Image, this same Being is now called Sun of Righteousness. And we see that the Father that begat Him proclaims that He will rise not on all, but only on those that fear His Name, giving them the light of the Sun of Righteousness as a reward for their fear. He, then, must be God the Word, Who said, "I am the Light of the world"; for He was "the light that lighteth every man coming into the world." […]
4:2.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 29

4:2.t:
And because his faith and devotion were invincible, the Lord revealed to him secret mysteries, touching the width of his thigh; because from his seed the Lord Jesus was to descend from the Virgin, who was neither unequal nor unequal to God; the width of the thigh signified the cross of him who astoundedly died, because the forgiveness of sin, spread throughout the whole world, would be beneficial to all who, astonished by their own body and given sleep, would grant resurrection to the dead. Hence not undeservedly rose the sun of holy Jacob, upon whose race the saving cross of the Lord shone brightly; for he is the sun of justice, who beholds God; for he is the eternal light.

But Jacob limped from his hip: For this reason, the sons of Israel do not eat the tendon to this day. […]
4:2.s: On Jacob and the Blessed Life

4:2.t: On the contrary, it is said what will befall those who fear the name of God: And for you who fear my name the Sun of justice will rise. He will judge all things truly, and will allow neither good things nor evil, neither virtues nor vices, to lie hidden. And healing will be in his wings, so that he may carry on his shoulders those healed through repentance, according to that which is written in Deuteronomy: Spreading out his wings he took them up, and carried them on his shoulders. Then those who are now shut up in the world as in a prison will go forth, and they will leap like calves from the herd, or like calves freed from their bonds. […]

Now the “horn of His people” is humble in afflictions, in tribulations, in temptations, in beating of the breast; when will He “exalt the horn of His people”? When the Lord hath come, and our Sun is risen, not the sun which is seen with the eye, and “riseth upon the good and the evil,” but That whereof is said, To you that hear God, “the Sun of Righteousness shall rise, and healing in His wings;” and of whom the proud and wicked shall hereafter say, “The light of righteousness hath not shined unto us, and the sun of righteousness rose not upon us.” This shall be our summer. Now during the winter weather the fruits appear not on the stock; thou observest, so to say, dead trees during the winter. He who cannot see truly, thinketh the vine dead; […]

And some are commanded to "be angry" after a wholesome fashion, but with our own selves, and with evil thoughts that arise, and "not to sin," viz., by bringing them to a bad issue. Finally, the next verse explains this to be the meaning more clearly: "The things you say in your hearts, be sorry for them on your beds:" i.e., whatever you think of in your hearts when sudden and nervous excitements rush in on you, correct and amend with wholesome sorrow, lying as it were on a bed of rest, and removing by the moderating influence of counsel all noise and disturbance of wrath. Lastly, the blessed Apostle, when he made use of the testimony of this verse, and said, "Be ye angry and sin not," added, "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath, neither give place to the devil." […]
4:2.s: The Twelve Books on the Institutes of the Coenobia, Book 8, Chapters 9-10

4:2.t: But unto you that fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings, and ye shall go forth and gambol as calves released from the stall.

Since, therefore, God is spiritual light, and Christ is called in the Scriptures Sun of Righteousness and Dayspring, the East is the direction that must be assigned to His worship. For everything good must be assigned to Him from Whom every good thing arises. Indeed the divine David also says, Sing unto God, ye kingdoms of the earth: O sing praises unto the Lord: to Him that rideth upon the Heavens of heavens towards the East. Moreover the Scripture also says, And God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there He put the man whom He had formed: and when he had transgressed His command He expelled him and made him to dwell over against the delights of Paradise, which clearly is the West. So, then, we worship God seeking and striving after our old fatherland.
4:2.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 12

4:2.t: In the allegorical sense, the sun signifies Christ. "The sun rises and the sun goes down." It rises in the nativity, it goes down in death; it orbits through noon in the ascension; it is inclined to the north in the judgment. Malachias refers to the first: "But for you who fear My name, there will arise the Sun of Justice with its healing rays."

4:3.t: Nor is he content with this end of joy, but he will tread down the impious when they are ash. Hence also there is this prayer for the just: And may God crush Satan under your feet swiftly. Abraham spoke to the Lord, perceiving that in comparison with the divine majesty he was ash: I am earth and ash; and therefore he will see the Sun of justice and will rest in the midst of his lots, and, carried by him, will be lifted up to the heavenly places. But he who through pride said: I will set my seat above the stars, I will be like the Most High, will be brought down to the earth, and will be like ash under the feet of the saints, when the day of the Lord who judges has come.

4:4.t: Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded him in Horeb for all Israel, precepts and judgements. LXX: likewise. In the future there will be a just retribution of deserts, when the devouring flame will consume and burn up the root and the shoot of the proud, and for those who fear the Lord the Sun of justice will rise, and healing in his wings. Therefore remember the law of Moses my servant, which I gave him on Mount Horeb, which is Sinai, for all Israel, precepts and judgements. But since the Apostle says: We know that the law is spiritual, and blessed David: Unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law; […]

After the prophecy, Malachi says, "Remember the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded him in Horeb for all Israel," and he makes a passing reference to "precepts and judgments." This emphasizes the declaration he had just made about the immense difference there is to be between the observers and the breakers of the law. The prophet's further purpose was that his readers might learn to give a spiritual interpretation to the law, finding in it Christ the judge who is to make the distinction between the good and the wicked. For it was not without reason that Christ said to the Jews, "If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote of me." […]

4:5.t: I fully expect these heretics to seize upon the example of Elijah as reincarnated in John the Baptist, and thus they would have become our Lord espousing the doctrine of reincarnation. "Elijah indeed has come, and they knew him not." And again, "And if you are willing to receive it, here is Elijah who was to come." Was the question of the Jews to John, "Are you Elijah?" to be understood in a Pythagorean sense and not in reference to the divine pronouncement: "Behold, I send you Elijah, the Tishbite"? But their theory of transmigration refers to the recall of a soul that had died long before and to its insertion in some other body. […]

We must after all this turn our attention to those scriptures also which forbid our belief in such a resurrection as is held by your Animalists (for I will not call them Spiritualists), that it is either to be assumed as taking place now, as soon as men come to the knowledge of the truth, or else that it is accomplished immediately after their departure from this life... Who has yet beheld Jesus descending from heaven in like manner as the apostles saw Him ascend, according to the appointment of the two angels? [Acts 1:11] Up to the present moment they have not, tribe by tribe, smitten their breasts, looking on Him whom they pierced. [John 19:37; Zechariah 12:10] No one has as yet fallen in with Elias; [Malachi 4:5] no one has as yet escaped from Antichrist; […]
4:5.s: On the Resurrection of the Flesh, Chapter 22

4:5.t: But since the Savior was the beginning of the resurrection of all people, it was fitting that the Lord alone should rise from the dead, by whom too the judgment is to enter the whole world, that they who have wrestled worthily may be also crowned worthily by him, by the illustrious Arbiter. [That is, he] himself first accomplished the course, and was received into the heavens, and was set down on the right hand of God the Father, and is to be manifested again at the end of the world as judge. It is a matter of course that his forerunners must appear first, as he says by Malachi and the angel, "I will send to you Elijah the Tishbite before the Day of the Lord, the great and notable day, comes; […]

Who of those who hear Jesus say of John, "If you wish to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come," would not inquire how John says to those who ask, "Are you Elijah?" "I am not"? Will he not also inquire how one ought to consider John himself to be Elijah who is to come, according to Malachi's statement: … "And behold, I am sending you Elijah the Tishbite before the great and renewed Day of the Lord comes, who will restore the heart of the father to his son and the heart of a man to his neighbor, lest I come and smite the earth utterly"?
4:5.s: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6:62

4:5.t: And what is the source of your belief that Elijah who is to come will baptize? He did not even baptize the wood on the altar in the times of Ahab, when it needed a bath that it might be burned up when the Lord appeared in the fire. He commanded the priests to do this, and not only once, for he says, "Do it a second time, when also they did it for a second time." And "Do it a third time, when also they did it a third time." How, then, will he who did not baptize at that time but gave the task to others, baptize when he has come in fulfillment of things said by Malachi? Christ therefore does not baptize in water but his disciples. He reserves for himself the act of baptizing with the Holy Spirit and fire.
4:5.s: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6:125

4:5.t: "And I saw another angel ascending from the east, having the seal of the living God" He speaks of Elias the prophet, who is the precursor of the times of Antichrist, for the restoration and establishment of the churches from the great and intolerable persecution. We read that these things are predicted in the opening of the Old and New Testament; for He says by Malachi: "Lo, I will send to you Elias the Tishbite, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, according to the time of calling, to recall the Jews to the faith of the people that succeed them." And to that end He shows, as we have said, that the number of those that shall believe, of the Jews and of the nations, is a great multitude which no man was able to number. […]
4:5.s: Victorinus Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

4:5.t: There are those who think that John is called Elijah for this reason: that, as at the second coming of the Savior, according to Malachi, Elijah is to go before and announce the judge who is to come, so John did at the first coming, and each is a messenger, either of the first coming of the Lord or of the second.

Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and he will turn the heart of the fathers to the sons, and the heart of the sons to their fathers, lest perhaps I come and strike the earth with anathema. LXX: Behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite, before the great and illustrious day of the Lord comes, who will turn the heart of the father to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbor, lest perhaps, coming, I strike the earth utterly. After Moses — whose commandments, as we have taught, are to be kept spiritually — he says that Elijah is to be sent, signifying by Moses the law and by Elijah prophecy, as Abraham says to a certain rich man clad in purple: They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them. […]

And the disciples asked him, saying: Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first? Unless we know the causes why the disciples asked about the name of Elijah, their question seems foolish and out of place. For what has it to do with the things written above, to ask about the coming of Elijah? It is a tradition of the Pharisees, according to the prophet Malachi, who is the last of the twelve, that Elijah will come before the coming of the Savior and turn back the heart of the fathers to the sons and of the sons to the fathers, and restore all things to their ancient state. […]
And behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite before the great and notable day of the Lord.

But Enoch and Elias the Thesbite shall be sent and shall turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, that is, the synagogue to our Lord Jesus Christ and the preaching of the apostles: and they will be destroyed by him.
4:5.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 26
